transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the plank roofs of Hollowmoot like it has every day for eleven years, turning the walkways between stilt-houses to black running mud. Under the dripping eave of the tallow-seller's stall, a soaked woman named Senna grips the sleeve of whoever stands nearest — her hands raw, her voice cracking as she begs. Her boy Corin followed the swarm-song three nights running, out past the Wardens' torches, out along the drowned causeway toward Saint Orrin's temple, and last night he didn't come home. She says the belltower still shows a light some nights, and that the Wardens have already written Corin's name on the burning-list, in case he comes back changed. She has nothing to pay with but a dry blanket and a promise to owe.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: Your boy heard something the Wardens fear to name—I see it in how they've already written his fate. Sit with me. What does this swarm-song sound like?

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (When Senna's raw fingers close around her sleeve, Ysolde doesn't pull away. She draws the desperate mother into a quieter corner, away from the press of the tallow-seller's stall and the worst of the rain. With the practical care of a galley cook, she takes Senna's torn hands and examines them—not roughly, but directly, the way she learned to see what others looked away from.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: The Wardens are wrong to write him off, Senna. The swamp doesn't take souls randomly—it calls to those who can hear it. I'll find Corin, or I'll find what took him. The rain remembers everything.

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (Aldous gently takes Senna's raw, shaking hands. Cold radiates from his fingers—the permanent chill of the drowned—and he meets her eyes with the absolute certainty of someone who has walked in death's shadow and lived. He glances toward the distant belltower where lamplight flickers through the endless rain.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: The Wardens won't burn him while I'm here. Tell me—when did the song start, and did Corin speak of anything else? Any words that weren't his own?

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (Morwen steps forward from the crowd beneath the eave, meeting Senna's raw red eyes. She doesn't offer empty comfort, just presence—and a question that cuts through to what matters.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Your boy isn't something to be burned yet. And he won't be, not if I find him first. I know that temple—I held the line before they decided I wasn't holding it right. Tell me everything he saw before he followed the song.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire closes her hand over Senna's, feeling the raw skin, the desperation in the grip. Her face hardens—not against Senna, but at the thought of the Wardens' cruelty, the same cruelty that cast her out and marked her as an enemy. She knows exactly what "burning-list" means. She's seen the Order's work before.)

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: The Wardens already know I'm here.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Morwen accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Senna's raw fingers tighten as she answers — the song started nine nights back, thin as wind through a broken flute, and it grew a chorus each night after. Corin spoke words that weren't his own, she says, drowned-slow syllables in a language she'd only ever heard chanted at Saint Orrin's before the flood took it. The belltower light isn't candlelight, she swears — it pulses, slow, like something breathing. Before anyone can press further, a horn sounds twice down the walkway and torchlight flares through the rain: a Warden patrol, and the man at the front is already pointing — he's placed Morwen's face from a dozen woodcuts nailed to Hollowmoot's posts. Senna shrinks back into the shadows, pulling her shawl over her head, and the choice sharpens fast — stay and be counted, or move now, toward the drowned temple and the boy, before the Wardens close the causeway behind them.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Torchlight smears gold through the downpour as the Warden patrol splashes up the walkway, boots slapping mud, the sergeant's pointing finger never wavering from Morwen's face. Behind him, two more Wardens fan out with hooked poles meant for pulling hive-touched from the water — tonight, meant for something else. Senna is already gone, swallowed by shadow and rain, and Corin's name is still chalked on the burning-list nailed to the post behind them. The sergeant shouts over the rain: known heretic, wanted for questioning, and the causeway gate will be barred within the hour on his order. Every second spent arguing is a second closer to that gate swinging shut.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: The boy's drowning either way, Sergeant. Don't let him drown because you followed orders you knew were wrong.

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde steps into the torchlight and rain, meeting the sergeant's eyes with the calm of someone who has read a hundred frightened men's hearts. She doesn't hide behind Morwen or bolt toward the temple—she stands in the mud between the Wardens and the causeway, steady as a stone in the current.)

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: I hear it in the rain—there's a lull coming through the downpour. Now. Run.

transcript.speaker: Aldous
transcript.text: (Aldous steps forward into the deluge, rain streaming from his soaked coat, and raises one hand as if conducting the storm itself. His fingers trace patterns in the air, and for a moment his eyes shine with something otherworldly—the mark of the drowned. The rain's rhythm shifts, hesitates. A passage is opening.)

transcript.text: You'll have to burn me first.

transcript.speaker: Morwen
transcript.text: (Morwen plants herself square in the sergeant's path, rain streaming down her face. She meets his pointing finger with a steady gaze, unmoving, her jaw set—not running, not yielding.)

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: Not on my watch. You try to close that gate and I stop you—permanently if I have to.

transcript.speaker: Mire
transcript.text: (Mire steps directly into the sergeant's path, rain hammering down between them. Her hand drops to her blade, and she meets his pointing finger with a glare forged in years of holding a line—first for the Wardens, now against them. She's not moving.)

transcript.text: You want to burn him? You burned me out first. This ends now.

The two spearmen flinch, hooked poles wavering between Morwen's unmoving glare and Ysolde's steady, reasonable voice still ringing in their ears — Doss's own mercy, thrown back at them, has them second-guessing the burning-list already. transcript.text: A quarter-mile on, the Ashwater Causeway simply ends — a black gap of open, rain-stitched water where the old stones have slumped beneath the flood, Saint Orrin's belltower a smudged shape beyond it. Aldous feels it first: the rain's rhythm gone wrong, too many splashes not falling from the sky. Shapes rise out of the reeds on both sides — hooked fishing spears, torn Wardens' sackcloth, eyes that don't blink against the rain. They don't speak. They come for the packs on your backs, for the dry food and rope strapped there, moving with the terrible patience of things that no longer feel the cold or the hooks in their own flesh.

transcript.text: I know what hunger sounds like. What is it you need?

transcript.speaker: Ysolde
transcript.text: (Ysolde steps forward into the gap between the group and the rising figures, rain streaming down her face. In the terrible patience of these creatures, in the jerking patience of their movements, she reaches for the echo of what they were: the private hunger that existed before the swarm-song, the part of them that still remembers wanting on their own.)

She goes down gasping onto broken stone—but even sprawled there, bleeding, she doesn't close her eyes. She listens, the way she's learned to listen a thousand times in a ship's galley: not with her ears, but with something deeper. To the jerking, uncoordinated movements of the creatures closing in. To the desperate raggedness beneath their movements. And beneath the drowned-slow chanting of the swarm-song, she hears it: hunger. Individual. Personal. The same hunger each of them carried before the song claimed them. For just a moment, it's enough—their own need pulls against the hive's command, fracturing their unity, making them twitch toward their own desperate want instead of the collective voice.)

ambiguities.issue: The rules state 'the GM may offer a compel on any player aspect or trouble whenever the story calls for it,' implying compels originate from the GM. Event 19 logs the compel with actor 'Mire' (self-compel on her own trouble 'Vengeance Over Sense'), and 'compel_forced': false, with no GM-side attribution in the log. The rules text does not address player-initiated (self) compels.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Treated as a valid compel: accepted, Mire gained 1 fate point (fp 3->4), and the complication (killing-stroke framing carried into event 23) was applied as if GM-offered.

ambiguities.issue: Opposition entries for named NPC 'Warden Sergeant Doss' are logged in a mixed passive/active format (e.g. '-1 (NPC - - - 0)', '+3 (NPC 0 - + +)') rather than clearly showing 4dF + a stated rating. The rules specify named NPCs roll 4dF + their own rating as active opposition, not the passive Average/+1-per-aspect ladder shown for unnamed threats.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The underlying NPC rating (+2) was reconstructed as internally consistent across events 20, 22, and 23 (dice sum + 2 = displayed opposition total in each case), so the rolls were accepted as correctly using active opposition despite the ambiguous notation.

ambiguities.issue: Event 21 (Aldous's create-advantage) lists a 'target_card': 'H-01' but no corresponding draw_id, cost entry, or narrated card-tag usage appears in the costs/compels list, so it's unclear whether a deck draw actually occurred for this advantage or whether the field is vestigial.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Not treated as a chargeable deck-draw cost since it has no draw_id or entry in the costs list; no card-tag compliance was assessed for it.

ambiguities.issue: The rules require 'The GM gets 1 fate point per player at the start of each scene; unspent points don't carry over.' With 4 players, the GM pool should be topped up to 4 at scene start. gm_fp is already 4 at event 28 (before the logged 'Scene 3 start' row at event 31) and stays flat at 4 through the whole scene with no explicit refill/reset row logged. There is no way to confirm whether this 4 is a fresh per-scene refresh or an un-cleared carryover from Scene 2.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Table treated the gm_fp value present at scene_start as the correct post-refresh value and did not require a separate logged refill event; GM fp compliance for scene 3 cannot be independently verified from the log.

ambiguities.issue: Events 28-30 and 62 (module_deploy, rail_add, rail_remove) reference a card-draw/rail/module subsystem (draw_id C-01, T-05, aspects tied to a 'rail') that is not defined anywhere in the supplied baseline Fate ruleset, so there is no section against which to check their legality (e.g., how many rail aspects a module may add, whether they count against the passive-opposition +4 cap, when they must be removed).
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Table treated the module/rail mechanic as an out-of-book extension and did not check it against any Fate section; it was allowed to run as logged.

ambiguities.issue: The only invented cost in the scene (event 53, for the tie at event 49) carries no draw_id, i.e. it was not built from a deck-drawn card, while the interim ruling AMB-19 elsewhere in this scene ties a similar mechanical event to 'the deck draw still happens.' The rules never specify whether GM-invented tie/fail costs are required to be seeded by a card draw or may be freely improvised.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Table allowed the tie cost at event 53 to be purely improvised narration with no card draw, since 'the GM invents costs' does not mandate a draw.

ambiguities.issue: The rules don't specify who has priority to spend a situation aspect's free invoke, or whether an actor may elect to pay a fate point instead of using an available free invoke on that same aspect. At event 84 the GM invokes A-1.4.10 (created at event 77 with 1 free invoke, per notes 'aspect A-1.4.10 (1 free)') and no prior event between 77 and 84 consumed that free invoke, yet gm_fp_spent shows 1 rather than 0.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Table treated the free invoke as optional rather than mandatory-first-use, letting the GM pay a fate point for the invoke while leaving the free invoke's status unresolved/unconsumed in the log.

ambiguities.issue: The rules don't say whether the same trouble aspect can be compelled twice on the same character within a single scene in quick succession (events 70 and 83, both 'Vengeance Over Sense' on Mire), nor whether a refused compel on the same trouble later in the scene should be treated any differently from a fresh compel.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: Table allowed a second compel on the identical trouble aspect within the same scene, applying normal accept/refuse fate-point mechanics independently each time.

ambiguities.issue: The rules say refusing a compel costs the player 1 fate point ('refuse = pay 1 fate point') but never state where that point goes. In event 104, Aldous refuses a compel and pays 1 fp (fp_change -1), but gm_fp stays at 4 both before and after — the point is not credited to the GM's pool or anywhere else visible in the log.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The table treated the refused-compel fee as simply removed from play rather than added to the GM's pool; gm_fp was left unchanged at 4.

ambiguities.issue: The compelled aspect text for event 104 ('Only survivor of the barge, marked by drowned ghosts') is not tagged with an aspect ID bracket like the invoked aspects elsewhere in the log (e.g. [MO-HC], [MO-A2], [MO-A3]), so it's unclear whether this is a formally sheet-registered aspect/trouble or an ad-hoc phrase improvised for the compel. Rules only permit compels on 'any player aspect or trouble.'
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The table accepted the untagged phrase as standing in for Aldous's trouble aspect and processed the compel normally.

cost_checks.note: This is a free/table compel with no draw_id and no card draw associated; the compel text 'Too Famous to Hide' was authored directly rather than pulled from a deck draw, so there is no drawn-card tag usage to verify.

This is a trouble-aspect compel with draw_id empty (no deck draw involved); its text is narrative flavor derived from the pre-existing trouble aspect 'Vengeance Over Sense,' not from a drawn card's tags, so drawn-card-tag usage is not applicable here.

Cost for the tie on event 49 (Morwen's attack) is a fully improvised GM narration (cost_mode/improvised=true, draw_id empty). No card was drawn or referenced, so no drawn-card tags were used in the cost text.
Free/improvised compel with draw_id empty — no card was drawn for this event, so tag usage from a drawn card is not applicable; text is GM-improvised.
Cost for event 105's success_major_cost result has draw_id empty and cost_mode 'improvised' — the GM wrote the cost narratively without drawing/using a card's tags.

friction.text: No aspect-creation or reveal event precedes the use of 'Too Famous to Hide' in the compel at event 10, making it hard to audit whether the aspect was actually live at the time.

The entire scene (events 4-12) contains zero dice rolls or skill checks, so most fate-economy rules (invokes, opposition ladder, outcomes) go untested this scene — only the single compel exercises the fate point economy.

GM fp sits unspent at 4 for the whole scene; since 'unspent points don't carry over,' worth confirming the engine actually resets/does not carry this balance into Scene 2 rather than just holding it static in this log.

The same aspect ('Vengeance Over Sense') was used both to pay off a compel (fp gain to Mire at event 19) and, two events later, as one of three paid invokes boosting Mire's attack roll (event 23) — the rules don't clarify whether a just-compelled trouble aspect can also be immediately paid-invoked by its owner in the same scene, forcing a case-by-case table call.

Opposition notation mixes a passive-ladder style prefix with an embedded 'NPC' dice string and a final total, requiring manual reconstruction of the NPC's actual skill rating to verify each roll rather than reading it directly off the log.
Whether compels can be self-initiated by a player (as Mire's was) versus requiring explicit GM framing is left open by the rules text, creating uncertainty for future logging/adjudication of compels.
No explicit 'GM fate point refill' row is logged at scene start, making the 'no carryover' fate-point rule unauditable from the log alone.

The module/rail card-deployment subsystem (events 28-30, 62) is exercised heavily in this scene but has no corresponding section in the supplied ruleset, so its legality can't be checked, only its arithmetic.

cost_mode is inconsistently populated ('improvised' only appears on event 49/53's tie; the fail at event 58 has no corresponding cost row or cost_mode at all, even though a fail nominally offers 'success at a major cost') — unclear if the player simply declined the option or if it went unlogged.

Morwen passed on every exchange in the scene (events 68, 74, 81) without invoking an aspect, spending a fate point, or rolling, leaving her fate-point total unchanged at 3 for the whole scene while others engaged and paid/gained points.

Mire's trouble aspect 'Vengeance Over Sense' was compelled twice back-to-back (accepted at event 70, refused at event 83), causing her fate points to oscillate 1→2→1 within a few exchanges, which added bookkeeping churn without changing the scene's trajectory.

The free-invoke-vs-paid-invoke ambiguity at event 84 (GM paying 1 fp for A-1.4.10 despite an apparently unused free invoke) forced a judgment call mid-session about invoke economy that the base rules don't resolve.

GM fate points stayed flat at 4 through the entire scene even though a compel was refused and a fate point was spent by Aldous, leaving the destination of that spent point unrecorded and making GM economy hard to audit.

Declared actions (events 92, 93, 102, 103) are logged as separate rows from their resolving rolls (96, 97, 105, 106) with no explicit parent/child linkage field, requiring manual text-matching to pair intent with outcome.

The invented cost text for event 105's major-cost success (event 107) has cost_valid left as null, so there is no recorded confirmation that the GM-authored complication was checked for proportionality before being applied.

free_text.best_moment: When Ysolde called to Corin's individual hunger beneath the swarm-song and broke through—"Corin, the swarm can wear your shape, but it can't wear your hunger." It felt like her core skill (deep listening, hearing what others hide) was exactly THE solution the story needed. No one else could have done that moment.
free_text.most_frustrating: Being spear-hooked repeatedly while trying to de-escalate and listen. I wanted her empathy and reasoning to work, but the hive was too strong and too hungry, and she ended bleeding from multiple wounds with a shoulder nearly split open. She tried to reach people through their hunger and got stabbed for it.
free_text.background_used: The "Exiled Cook of the Night-Barge Who Hears Everything" concept was used *extensively* and felt core to everything—finding cracks in the swarm-song through individual hunger, reaching Corin, holding the breach open. This landed really well. It wasn't just flavor; it was the actual solution. The "Cast out by the Stiltfolk Clans" and "Sworn to ruin the traitor" aspects didn't come up, which is fine for one session, but they felt sidelined.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to reach Corin more directly and offer real comfort, not just listen from a distance while others fought. Also wanted her attempts to de-escalate conflict to actually *work* more—to talk her way through instead of always ending in bloodshed. But the hive-song and the creatures' hunger were too absolute.
free_text.one_sentence: Her listening ability was woven into every major moment and felt vital, not incidental, which was satisfying—but everything cost her blood, and she ended the session badly wounded with her other aspects untouched.

free_text.best_moment: Finding and revealing the processional path through the drowned temple—the one reading only I could make, using my fortune-teller's sight to see what the faithful had walked into stone beneath the swarm's blind hunger.
free_text.most_frustrating: The moment I named the hive's weakness and became its marked target, I got sidelined by a hookspear while the others did the real work of escape and rescue.
free_text.background_used: yes, good - my fortune-teller abilities were essential throughout, and being marked by drowned ghosts gave me the second sight the moment demanded. Even my vow showed up as context, grounding why I was in that temple at all.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: A genuine moment to negotiate or turn one of the hive-touched through words rather than just supporting Ysolde's empathy or fighting alongside Mire—I wanted to read *people* the way I read rain and swarm-song.
free_text.one_sentence: My fortune-teller's gifts were the key to reading the swarm's weakness, right up until they made me the hive's marked target.

free_text.best_moment: When Morwen stepped between Ysolde and the last stalker saying "Not her"—that moment of quiet, absolute conviction with the blade coming up felt perfectly true to the character and hit emotionally hard.
free_text.most_frustrating: The major-cost stumble where my own strike's force knocked me back into the water felt deflating, but it was mechanically fair and kept the tension high.
free_text.background_used: All five aspects were clearly woven in: my fame made the Wardens recognize me, the hive-possessed Corin forced me to confront my core doubt about souls, and my vow to stand against the Wardens' torches was directly tested. This landed really well—the GM clearly understood the character and built scenes around these tensions.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: More opportunities to voice Morwen's actual philosophical doubt about whether hive-touched have souls. The session explored hunger, consciousness, and resistance within the swarm beautifully, but I wanted Morwen to explicitly wrestle with what she was fighting.
free_text.one_sentence: My backstory wasn't just acknowledged—it was the foundation of every scene, and the GM created situations specifically designed to test the contradictions in my vows and doubts.

free_text.best_moment: When Ysolde got badly speared and I said "Not one of mine falls"—stepping into full line-guard stance to protect her felt like the absolute core of who Mire is, someone who doesn't abandon people even when it's dangerous.
free_text.most_frustrating: Ysolde getting hit by that hookspear despite my attempts to protect everyone—the feeling that Mire's commitment to holding the line means she has to keep putting herself in harm's way rather than tactical retreat.
free_text.background_used: Yes. The disgrace, Verrick's betrayal, the orphanage training, the temple I used to guard—all used well. The compels from "Vengeance Over Sense" and "marked enemy of the Causeway Wardens" felt organic and created real narrative weight, not forced.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted more dialogue with the hive-touched creatures, to understand what they were before the swarm took them. The pacing pushed toward combat, and Mire's instincts did too. Also wanted a moment for Mire to process fighting at the temple she used to guard.
free_text.one_sentence: The tension between "still holds the line" and "disgraced outcast" was executed really well—it gave Mire genuine weight and made every choice feel costly.

chronicle.summary: Torn from a hookspear ambush and a fevered march through the drowned nave, the party pulled Corin free of the swarm's stolen skin, learning that the hive's song could fracture when it tried to hold a soul and heal itself at once. Blood-soaked and half-drowned, Ysolde, Aldous, Morwen, and Mire cut down the Hive-Touched Pack that answered the belltower's call, breaking the swarm's shared body with one final blow before its master ever fully woke. They fled down a processional path older than the hive's hunger, dragging Corin and their wounds into the rain — free of the nave, but marked now as the ones who silenced the Hive Mother's children and made her open her eye.
